The harmony determines how many suits must be played in the trick—not being able to is considered playing “off-harmony,” making that player ineligible for points. At the end of the trick, the player who played the highest on-harmony card scores two points, and the lowest on-harmony card scores for the value of that card (those bass notes are so important!). Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Vivo 1.1 Overview 1.2 Components 1.3 Card Types 1.3.1 Playing Cards 1.3.2 Harmony Cards 1.4 Setup 1.5 Playing a Trick 1.6 Following the Harmony 1.6.1 Forced New Suit 1.6.2 Impossible Harmony 1.7 Playing Off-Harmony 1.8 Scoring a Trick 1.8.1 Score Highest 1.8.2 Score Lowest 1.8.3 Discard 1.9 Tie Breakers 1.9.1 All Cards Tie 1.10 Next Trick 1.11 Round End 1.12 Game End 1.13 Clarifications 1.14 Strategy Tips 1.15 Credits Vivo Overview Vivo is a trick-taking card game of harmony, timing, and precise suit play. The game is played over 2 rounds , each consisting of 12 tricks . In each trick: Players must collectively play the exact number of suits shown on the current Harmony card , if possible. At the end of the trick: The player who played the highest rank scores The player who played the lowest rank scores After 2 rounds: The player with the most points wins. Harmonize with other players to hit the right notes and play a perfect puppy performance! Components 48 Playing cards 4 suits Ranks 1–12 15 Harmony cards Card Types Playing Cards Each card has: Suit Rank Ranks range from: 1–12 --- Harmony Cards Harmony cards show how many suits must appear during the current trick. Possible harmonies: Solo = 1 suit Duet = 2 suits Trio = 3 suits Quartet = 4 suits Setup Grab a pen and paper for scoring. Remove cards based on player count. Players Remove 3 Remove any 1 suit 4 Use all 4 suits Harmony card adjustments: Players Remove Harmony Cards 3 Remove 1 Solo, 1 Duet, 1 Trio 4 Remove all 3 Quartets Shuffle the Harmony cards. Reveal 1 Harmony card face-up in the center. Place remaining Harmony cards in a face-down pile. Reveal the next Harmony card face-up beside the pile. Shuffle the Playing cards. Deal each player 12 cards . The player who most recently sang a song leads the first trick. Playing a Trick The lead player: Plays any card from their hand. Then, moving clockwise: Each player plays 1 card. Players must follow the harmony if possible. Following the Harmony On your turn: Count how many different suits have already been played this trick. === If the required number of suits has already been played: You must play: One of the suits already played === If the required number of suits has NOT yet been played: You may play: Any suit Provided the required number of suits can still be completed by the end of the trick. Forced New Suit If the harmony can only be completed by introducing a new suit: You must play a new suit. Impossible Harmony If the required harmony cannot be completed regardless of what you play: You must still play a new suit. Playing Off-Harmony If you have no cards that follow the harmony: You must play off-harmony To play off-harmony: Choose any card Play it face-up as normal Important: Off-harmony cards are ignored during scoring Off-harmony players cannot score points Scoring a Trick After everyone has played: Ignore all off-harmony cards. Then resolve scoring: Score Highest The player who played the highest rank: Flips their card face-down Adds it to their scoring row Each facedown card will be worth: 2 points Score Lowest The player who played the lowest rank: Keeps their card face-up Adds it to their scoring row Each face-up card is worth: Its printed rank Discard All other played cards: Are discarded face-down Each player keeps their scored cards in a scoring row. Tie Breakers If players tie for: Highest rank OR Lowest rank The player who played later in the trick wins the tie. All Cards Tie If all players tie: The tie winner scores as highest rank No player

[Rating: 1/10] Strange trick taking game where the style of the trick changes each turn. In practice it's a much more basic straightforward trick taking game than the rules would implies, as such it's fine, good even. With the randomness of the harmony cards dictating the must/must not follow rules for the trick combined with 2 players always scoring each trick, it feels like an exercise in not short suiting yourself to remain viable to play in every trick thus avoiding any lost opportunities to score. Playing from that perspective should be interesting as you weigh your cards for short term scoring possibil

[Rating: 3/10] Overview: A trick-taking game where players collectively play the exact number of suits shown on a harmony card each trick. The highest and lowest cards both score points equal to their rank.  What I dislike: - One is mostly just checking whether the harmony rules force playing a new suit or following an existing one. Not much real decision making. - Drawing middle ranks like 5s through 8s leaves one unable to compete for either high or low, and there's no way to fix it. Does everything that game does, but [i]slightly[/i] better. More interesting scoring parameters, which creates a strange inverse-bell curve value of the cards. The lowest cards and the highest cards appear to be the best, with the mid-rank cards having the most difficult trim winning a trick. (N.B. [Rating: 4/10] To me this seems fairly chaotic and would need extensive card counting to be even a little bit helpful. So played on vibes and keeping your options open, and need to accept the huge swings that come from the mostly unpredictable 'low card wins'.

[Rating: 5/10] A trick taking game where players are trying to follow the rule of the round, either solo/duet/trio/quartet (each restriction meaning a 1/2/3/4 different suit(s)). The latter player(s) is on the hook with being forced to follow the rules. Only players that follow the restrictions have a chance to win the trick. The highest card played will score 2 points. The lowest card played will gain face value. After 2 rounds, the player with the most points wins.

[Rating: 5/10] A four-player hand of VIVO has an uncommon rhythm to it.  Early on, the cards played first and second will often have little chance of being either high or low (the cards that score points in each trick).  This is because each trick the flip of a card determines the number of suits that must be played to it (one to four).  In a trick that demands anything other than a single suit, my early 1 or 12 can be beaten by the same number of a different suit. [Rating: 5/10] Played this once with 3 players and didn't like it. The first round I was 'played' and had a terrible score. But for some strange idiotic reason there are only 2 rounds, which means one bad round = you are out, Sir! There are far better trick taking games out there, so don't need to play this one again.
